title: State Subsidies Subside Further
gist: Gavekal Dragonomics argues that the subsidies Western politicians attack — local-government tax breaks and direct budget support to Chinese manufacturers — have shrunk significantly since 2022 as local fiscal budgets tightened, while the real channel of Chinese industrial policy has shifted to privileged access to equity capital, which is reaccelerating for favored sectors like semiconductors.

insights.claim: Financial reports of listed Chinese companies show that the government support most likely to originate from local governments has declined significantly since 2022, a casualty of tight local budgets and shifting political priorities.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Margin support for Chinese industrial exporters is thinner than the Western political debate assumes — screen listed-company subsidy line items rather than headline policy rhetoric when modelling Chinese manufacturer profitability.
insights.quote: The financial reports of listed companies show that the support most likely to come from local governments has declined significantly since 2022, a casualty of tight budgets and changing political priorities.
insights.locator: What’s the reality behind this conflicting rhetoric?

insights.claim: The government support that remains for Chinese companies is still sizable but is now driven mainly by central-government policies, and is therefore unlikely to shrink dramatically.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate the local-subsidy decline into a broad withdrawal of Chinese state support; the centrally directed floor under favored industries persists and keeps competitive pressure on Western rivals.
insights.quote: The remaining benefits are still sizable, but are more driven by central-government policies and are unlikely to shrink dramatically.
insights.locator: The remaining benefits are still sizable

themes.theme: Equity capital as the new industrial-policy channel

insights.claim: The main channel of Chinese industrial policy is no longer tax benefits or direct subsidies from the government budget but privileged access to equity capital for favored companies.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Track Chinese equity issuance and state-linked fund allocations, not fiscal subsidy line items, to identify which sectors Beijing is actually backing — and note that trade remedies aimed at subsidies may miss the real support mechanism.
insights.quote: The main channel of Chinese industrial policy is no longer tax benefits or direct subsidies from the government budget, but privileged access to equity capital.
insights.locator: The main channel of Chinese industrial policy

insights.claim: Equity financing for favored Chinese sectors, particularly semiconductors, is picking up again.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A reacceleration of equity funding into Chinese semiconductors points to another capacity build in chips — bearish for pricing in commoditized chip segments and a signal to watch Chinese semi-cap and foundry issuance pipelines.
insights.quote: And equity financing for favored sectors, particularly semiconductors, is picking up again.
insights.locator: And equity financing for favored sectors

insights.claim: Beijing denies that any systemic overcapacity exists while simultaneously claiming to crack down on illegal local-government subsidies as part of a campaign against wasteful investment and destructive competition — a contradiction Gavekal tests against listed-company financials rather than accepting either side's rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Both the Western 'subsidy' narrative and Beijing's denial are unreliable guides; company-level disclosure is the tradeable source of truth on how much state support Chinese exporters actually receive.
insights.quote: Beijing denies that there is any systemic overcapacity, but says it is cracking down on illegal subsidies by local governments as part of its campaign to prevent wasteful investment and destructive competition
insights.locator: The political backlash in the US and Europe

insights.claim: US and European political backlash against trade with China centers on manufacturing subsidies and industrial-policy support alleged to cause unfair competition and excess capacity.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Tariff and trade-defense risk for China-exposed manufacturers is anchored on the subsidy argument, so evidence that direct subsidies are fading could reshape the legal basis of future countervailing-duty cases.
insights.locator: The political backlash in the US and Europe
